doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Buddy Rich, Mel Lewis and Thad Jones: high school, college, life
summary: Rich played even when sick; saxophone technique learned in his band; first New York gig with Mel and Thad; summed up as high school, college, life.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: sounds like Buddy’s not a very nice human being. But I could dig him because when he was sick he played. Even though he had a sub, he had Mel Lewis on the bus. Mel didn’t play one note.
So he wouldn’t ask you do to anything that he wouldn’t do.

That’s right. That’s what I got from him. You know what I mean? So to me that’s what I mean, I mean he’s crazy but I could dig it. I mean technically, on that band you played much more notes. I don’t mean complicated but for me as a saxophone player I learned a lot about the saxophone technique because of some of the music he played. It was like hard, another step. Okay? And then with Mel and Thad, when I got to New York, I mean I knew Thad. I met Thad at Youngstown. Tony Leonardi got Thad to come to Youngstown. So I used to sub on the band. My first gig in New York was with Mel and Thad, but it wasn’t the big band, it was a quintet. So that flipped me out. That was my first gig.
You said something yesterday, you said you learned more on that gig on the first few weeks than you did in college. What do you learn on that first — I mean what was so memorable?

Well just what the thing sounded like around you. You know, and how they handled, I mean these were masters of playing jazz music. And I’m just out of college. And Tony Leonardi was great, believe me, I mean I learned a lot from him. But now this is experiencing it. That’s what I mean. Even with now you say about the band with Thad and Mel or the Mel Lewis band, that was more like real life. I mean he dealt with a lot — you know it’s in your home town which is now New York, you go to work and just the music was so ridiculously challenging at the time especially, and you’re with Thad Jones and Mel Lewis and everybody else in the band, when I was subbing, it was Pepper Adams, you know Jerry Dodgion, you know what I mean? All these guys. I said what? Bob Brookmeyer. You know I mean I’m a kid. So for a summation, and I don’t want to make this sound weird, because it’s not like this, but just to compare it I would say Woody was like high school, Buddy was like college, and Mel was like life. You know what I mean? That’s the way I would answer your question, even though it took me a half hour to answer your question.
